title: Triangles

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Eighth Saying: Three angles that add to two right angles are the only gossip worth believing.*

The salt flat lay out before them, a blinding white expanse that stretched into the distance, unbroken by any tree or stone. Vasht stood in the center of a small circle of driven pegs, holding a length of braided hemp string that he had tied to the first peg. He looked less like a master surveyor and more like a man preparing to hang a very heavy picture frame.

"Triangulation," he said, his voice carrying easily in the thin air. "The baseline is our anchor. It is the one thing we know for certain. But we cannot walk to every hill and measure it with a chain. We would be here until the world wore out." He pulled the string taut to the second peg. "So we use angles. Given one side, and two angles, the rest of the triangle is forced. It has no choice. It must follow."

Isla set up the sightglass on the tripod at the first station. The brass instrument gleamed in the harsh sunlight, its lenses catching the glare. She adjusted the fine screws, her hands steady, while Mags sat on a flat slab of rock nearby, a piece of charcoal in hand, scratching figures onto the dusty surface.

"Law of sines," Mags muttered, tapping the charcoal against the stone. "Sine of A over side a, equals sine of B over side b. It’s elegant. It’s also terrifying if you get the units wrong."

"Units are the only thing that matters," Vasht said, tightening the string. "The geometry does not care about your feelings. It cares about the sine."

Isla looked through the glass, aligning the crosshairs with a distant hummock that had a small cairn of stones on it. "I have the bearing. Ready."

"Read," Vasht said.

She turned the vernier scale, her eye sharp, her hand a whisper of motion. "Forty-two degrees, twelve minutes, zero seconds."

Mags wrote it down. The number sat on the stone, solid and true. The land settled beneath their feet, no longer a drifting uncertainty but a problem that could be solved.
pages.image: On a vast white salt flat, Isla in a mustard-yellow canvas coat kneels beside a brass sightglass on a tripod, looking intently at a distant stone cairn, while Master Vasht, in a grey wool coat and felt hat, tautens a length of hemp string between wooden pegs nearby.

pages.text:
Joss Harrowgate did not like waiting. While the others debated the theoretical underpinnings of trigonometry, he was already moving, his boots crunching loudly on the salt crust. He had a carpenter’s pencil behind one ear and a coil of rope over his shoulder, and he looked at the nearest cluster of low hummocks with the critical eye of a man inspecting a defective batch of timber.

"We need stations," he announced, swinging the rope. "You can’t angle to a hill that’s drifting. You need a flag. A bright one. Something that says, 'I am here, I am fixed, and I am not going anywhere.'"

He picked a spot on the highest of the three nearby mounds. It was a tenuous balance of rock and loose salt, the sort of ground that would crumble under a heavy boot.

"Brace it," Isla said, watching him climb.

Joss grinned, a quick, sharp expression. "A triangle is the only shape that cannot be pushed out of itself. Rectangles flex. Circles roll. But a triangle? It’s got integrity." He drove three thick poles into the base of the mound, tying them together with a knot so tight it looked angry. "If the ground shifts, this holds. If the wind blows, this holds. If the world tries to bend me, I bend the world."

He lashed a bundle of poles upward, creating a narrow tower that rose above the salt haze. He climbed it with the ease of a cat on a fence, then dropped a square of bright crimson cloth over the top. It fluttered in the thin air, a vivid splash of color against the pale, endless white.

"There," he said, dropping down and brushing salt from his rust-red shirt. "Ten miles visibility. Maybe more. It’s ugly, but it works."

Isla looked at the tower, then at the other two spots he had marked. "You built the frame before the measurement. That’s... practical."

"Precision is a luxury," Joss said, wiping his hands on a rag. "A signal is a necessity. You need to see what you’re measuring before you can measure it." He tapped the braced base. "Hold that thought."
pages.image: Joss Harrowgate, a tall boy with sandy hair and a rust-red shirt, climbs a tall, narrow tower of lashed poles on a white salt hummock, holding a bright red cloth aloft, while Isla watches from below in her mustard coat, her expression a mix of skepticism and admiration.

pages.text:
The first station was a test of endurance. The sun climbed higher, baking the salt into a shimmering haze that distorted the horizon. Isla sat in the shade of the tripod, her eye pressed to the brass sightglass, her body still as a statue.

"Ready?" Mags asked, holding the field-book open.

"Ready."

Isla read the angle to the red flag. She read it again. Then she read it a third time, averaging the numbers in her head before speaking. "Forty-two, twelve, zero. Forty-two, twelve, one. Forty-two, twelve, zero. Average is forty-two, twelve, zero."

Mags wrote it down. The ink dried almost instantly in the dry air.

They moved to the second angle, the one pointing back to the baseline. This was the harder one. The baseline was long, and the distance was great. Isla adjusted the screw, watching the crosshairs dance across the salt.

"Fifty-seven, thirty, twelve," she said.

"And the third angle?" Vasht asked, standing behind her with his hat tipped low.

The sum of the angles in a triangle is always one hundred and eighty degrees. She had measured two from the baseline; Joss and Mags carried the sightglass out to the red flag, and she read the third from there.

"Eighty, nineteen, forty-eight," she said softly.

Vasht nodded. "And the sum?"

"One hundred and eighty degrees," Isla said. "And two minutes of arc."

The silence that followed was heavy. Two minutes of arc. It was a tiny amount, invisible to the naked eye, but in the world of the surveyor, it was a chasm. It meant the triangle was not closed. It meant something was wrong.

"Where did the two minutes go?" Isla asked, her voice tight.

Vasht did not answer. He simply waited, his grey eyes fixed on the distant red flag. He knew, of course. They all knew. The land was loose. The angles were not static. They were drifting, slowly, like the hills themselves. And Isla had to find out where they were drifting to.
pages.image: Isla, in her mustard-yellow coat, leans intensely into a brass sightglass, her eye narrowed in concentration, while Mags Okoro, in a teal jacket and blue scarf, holds a field-book steady nearby, her face tense with worry as they stand on the white salt flat.

pages.text:
Vasht took the field-book from Mags’ hands, his movement deliberate and final, and he did not look at Isla, though he could likely feel the specific, humming tension of a mind trying to find a flaw that might not exist.

"Look at the shape," he said, pointing to the network of lines Isla had sketched on the plane-table. "See how the angles are arranged? This is a thin triangle. A needle. In a strong figure, the angles are wide. They share the load of the error. In a thin one, the error is concentrated. It magnifies."

Isla looked at her sketch, where the lines were long and narrow, stretched out across the salt flat like taut strings, and she realized she had chosen the stations because they were the highest points with the best visibility, not because she had considered the geometry. She had not thought about the shape.

"Redraw it," Vasht said.

Isla picked up her pencil and erased the lines, leaving faint grey marks on the paper that she had to look at very closely to see. She studied the map, checking the positions of the hummocks and the distance to the next ridge, then moved the station on the left closer to the center, which made the triangle wider and the angles more equal.

"Better," Vasht said. "But not enough. Move the other one."

She shifted the second point, and the network began to look less like a stretch and more like a weave, forming a lattice of strong, sturdy triangles that supported one another.

Joss leaned over the table, his nose almost touching the paper. "It looks like a cat’s cradle."

"It is better than a cat’s cradle," Vasht said, his voice dry. "A cat’s cradle is a toy. This is a structure. It holds. It is strong. And it is honest."

Isla looked at the new network, which was elegant and efficient and true, and she felt a strange sense of satisfaction, like the feeling of a well-tempered instrument, a feeling of having built something that would stand.

"Okay," she said, her voice steady. "Let’s measure it."
pages.image: Isla, in her mustard coat, crouches over a plane-table on a folding wooden desk, carefully drawing a new network of lines with a pencil, while Master Vasht, in his grey coat, stands behind her pointing at the sketch, and Joss leans in with a curious expression.

pages.text:
The calculation spilled across the flat stone, Mags’ charcoal moving with a quick, rhythmic scratch that sounded like rain on a tin roof. The numbers were long and intricate, a cascade of sines and cosines that defied the small, dusty rectangle of rock. Isla watched the figures stack up, her eyes tracking the arithmetic as if following a thread through a loom, waiting for the pattern to resolve.

"Eleven miles," Mags said, her voice rising with the particular brightness of a number that had come out clean. "And two hundred and fourteen links."

Isla stared at the result, her fingers twitching against the edge of the stone. Eleven miles was a full day’s walk, a distance that usually required a map, a compass, and a great deal of doubt. They were standing on the grey expanse of the salt flat, looking at a red flag planted on a distant hummock, and yet they knew, with absolute certainty, exactly how far away it was.

"That’s... that’s impossible," she said, the words feeling clumsy in her mouth.

"Why?" Vasht asked. He was watching her, his grey eyes calm and patient behind the brim of his felt hat.

"Because we haven’t walked it. We haven’t measured it with a chain. We just... thought it."

Vasht smiled, a small, faint curve of the mouth that did not reach his eyes but seemed to settle into them. "That is the point. The land is loose, Isla. It drifts. But the math is true. The math holds. If the angles are correct, and the baseline is true, then the distance is real. It is there, whether we can see it or not. The geometry does not care about our doubt; it only cares about the consistency of the data."

A cold, sharp sensation moved through her, not quite fear but a profound, vibrating awe. It was the feeling of a well-oiled mechanism engaging, the quiet, unyielding truth of the triangle locking into place. She looked at the red flag, then at the chalk dust on her fingers, and felt the strange lightness of a problem solved before it had even been walked.

"I’m going to pace it," she said, her voice steadying as she picked up her brass compass. "A loose check. Just to see."

She turned and began the walk, her boots crunching on the crystalline surface of the flat. It was a long, tedious, repetitive walk, the sun beating down on her neck and the horizon stretching out in every direction, indifferent and vast. But as she reached the base of the mound, wiping the sweat from her brow, and looked up at the red flag, the distance resolved. She had measured it. She had found it. And the land, for the first time, had listened.
pages.image: Isla, in her mustard-yellow coat and brown boots, walks across the white salt flat toward a distant hummock with a red flag, her posture upright and determined, while in the background, Mags and Vasht watch from the base, the vast expanse of salt stretching to the horizon.

words: determining location by measuring angles from known points
a scale for measuring small differences with high precision
weak, flimsy, or barely holding together
the ability to withstand hardship or difficult conditions
a grid-like structure of intersecting lines or bars
